Sensation. The biological and psychological process by which sensory receptors detect stimuli from the environment and transmit signals to the nervous system. It is the first stage of perception, distinct from the conscious interpretation of sensory data. Sensation underlies all human awareness of heat, light, sound, taste, smell, and touch.

The process begins with transduction, the conversion of physical or chemical stimuli like photons, pressure waves, and chemical molecules into electrical signals the nervous system can process. The five classical senses—vision, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—are complemented by proprioception, body position awareness, and the vestibular system, which governs balance and motion. Absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity required to produce a sensation at least fifty percent of the time. It varies by sense and individual sensitivity. Sensory adaptation occurs through repeated exposure to unchanging stimuli. The nervous system suppresses constant background signals, reducing the perceived intensity. Taste and smell are chemoreceptive senses, responding to dissolved or airborne molecules. The tongue and olfactory epithelium have specialized receptor types for sweet, salty, bitter, sour, and savory, called umami. Touch involves distinct receptors for pressure, temperature, and pain, distributed across the skin. Density varies by body region, explaining why fingertips are more sensitive than forearms. The Scoville scale quantifies spiciness, a pure sensation of pain triggered by capsaicinoids in peppers, independent of flavor. All of these sensory systems rely on the nervous system's processing of sensory signals, and sensation forms the foundation of perception, the cognitive interpretation of sensory data. Sensation also engages proprioception and the vestibular system in creating our sense of space and body position.
